# Camera recovery status

The polygon-by-polygon interpolation approach is rejected. Partial interpolation produced inconsistent motion, and projected-polygon matching did not establish stable object identity. Do not describe those builds as a finished 60-fps solution. The synchronized 4K build with original timing remains the stable fallback.

The road pipeline is now traced further upstream: 030027F0 invokes 03000D48 to transform 68-byte source records, then 03001800 prepares/clips projected data, followed by 030032F0 rasterization. At 03000D48 the shared camera is at game_state +54 (pointer); camera fields +00/+08/+18/+20 are fixed-point X/Z transform coefficients, and +24/+28/+2C are translation/height terms. World records come from game_state +10 with 68-byte stride. Optional source +2A index addresses 32-byte offset records through game_state +18. Transformed destination records have 52-byte stride at game_state +68. These are observed interfaces for the inspected ROM, not yet a complete scene format.

native_camera.c reproduces the integer memory-output contract of 03000D48, including 32-bit arithmetic wrapping, optional offsets, cyclic endpoint links, and early far-depth culling. 1000 randomized comparisons against original ARM code passed, including 523 far-cull cases. This file is not integrated into a new player executable and does not itself produce smooth animation.

Next: recover clipping/projection and stable world-face/material relationships, retain world geometry, then render a complete scene through a shared interpolated camera. Keep game simulation at original timing. Never fall back to matching unrelated screen polygons as a substitute for this work.

## Native rigid motion layer

rigid_motion.c/h now implements camera-independent object poses and a shared camera pose in double precision. Q14 rotation decoding removes fixed-point scale/shear error using orthonormal axes, then converts to a unit quaternion. Presentation uses shortest-path quaternion interpolation and linear world-position interpolation. Every vertex in a scene sample receives the same phase. Object vertices transform into world space first, then through the sampled camera. The recovered camera's world position is the negative of its stored translation; its rotation maps world axes to camera axes. This distinction avoids rotating the camera offset in the wrong order.

The module only consumes captured poses and geometry. It does not write emulated memory, advance gameplay, project polygons, or replace the host renderer. It clamps interpolation phase, rejects non-finite inputs and degenerate/reflected rotation matrices, and handles opposite quaternion signs and the +179/-179 degree boundary. Fixed-point matrices are normalized intentionally; this is a rigid presentation path, not an exact substitute for the integer reference routines.

Validation: 1,000 independent rotation-decode cases passed (maximum unit-vector error 0.0000452 after Q14 quantization); 1,000 randomized camera/object scene samples preserved model dimensions within 8.2e-12 world units. Captured driving data supplied 49 poses. Using their actual refresh timestamps produced 174 intermediate intervals with changed model vertex positions. All 11,544 live model-distance checks stayed within 1.84e-12 world units. These are pre-projection mathematical tests, not visual proof of wobble-free gameplay. They do not test clipping, material changes, scene visibility or GPU pacing.

Next: retain complete world/model topology and materials, integrate the shared pose sampler into the native scene renderer, and validate full-scene visual motion at normal game timing. No new player executable was issued in this step.

## 2026-10-04 active goal: bounded cross-thread submission ownership

Implemented submission_handoff.c/h: three-entry FIFO protected by Windows critical section. Successful push clears producer pointer and transfers sole ownership; full/stale/closed rejection leaves caller pointer intact. Pop transfers ownership to consumer. Monotonic nonzero epoch changes drain only queued entries; already popped frames remain consumer-owned. Close rejects subsequent pushes and drains pending entries. Destroy requires all users joined; no unsafe concurrent destructor promise. Queue never calls bridge capture/read APIs. Production host integration not yet enabled.

Helper build PASS. Extended real-packet component test PASS100 transfers across actual simultaneous producer/consumer threads. Every received complete native packet/HUD/time/camera/source/zero bundle compares exactly with original retained frame. Existing real capture eviction/checkpoint reload and final original EWRAM-IWRAM parity still PASS. Reports now write fresh RUNNING/FAIL to prevent stale queue successes. Archived sources/build/test reports.

This supplies a concrete bounded ownership transfer prerequisite, not a concurrent GL renderer or smooth60fps claim. ### Captured native HUD cost checkpoint (2026-10-07)
Measured the existing obj-tile.dll prepared OBJ/window routine over all 160 rows of seven complete captured scenes (8758, 8762, 8766, 8769, 8773, 8776, 8780). After one warmup, three repetitions per scene produced identical candidate color/tag/control/backdrop hashes. Median total native-call times were 0.4439–0.5508 ms per scene, including ctypes call overhead. Private OBJ VRAM copies are measured separately in result.json. Evidence and tested input hashes: checkpoints/captured-hud-native-cost-20261007.
This is a captured component benchmark, excluding live scheduling, layer_read, text input extraction, cache copies and GPU composition. It does not establish 60-fps gameplay or exclusive stall causality. It gives no reason to assume OBJ arithmetic alone explains the previously observed 11.9276-ms live HUD input stage. Next dependency: profile owned snapshot reads, text extraction and HUD input/cache copies in that stage before changing OBJ algorithms.
The spatial sky candidate remains isolated from the playable launcher: fractional movement, wrap and full-pixel parity component checks pass, while its latest 30-second live cadence test still has seven active-play gaps above 33.333 ms. Overall project estimate remains approximately 65%, with high uncertainty; native full-scene timing, fidelity and physical controller/display verification remain incomplete.

### Process-based source-pair preparation rejected by full-scene timing (2026-10-11)

The permission-enabled test-only process-preparation candidate completed a 30-second hidden-window full-scene plus continuously interpolated sky run (`work/camera/prototype-runs/owned-native-1791717156948054800.json`). Its child process and shared output mapping shut down cleanly (exit code 0; no forced termination; mappings and renderer resources released), and the real refresh-8754 sky in-place/immutable byte comparison passed. It is nevertheless a clear regression and is rejected for live use: 1,341 original updates (22.452 simulated seconds) in 30.017 wall seconds, 353 scene submissions, and 1,348 presentation attempts. Presentation-gap p95/p99/max were 75.75/99.79/156.81 ms, with 350 intervals over 33.333 ms; original-update lateness p95 reached about 7.12 seconds. The smoke runner correctly reports `smooth_60fps_verified=false`.

Process telemetry identifies concrete costs. Across 352 source-pair jobs, the child batch took median 40.49 ms (p95 60.28, max 143.94) for four alpha samples; median child precomputation was 19.96 ms and encoding 9.68 ms. The parent decoded the returned batch in median 8.65 ms (p95 17.28). Each result represented median 24.91 MiB of original sample data and 7.78 MiB transferred through shared output; shared write/read each added roughly 2.8 ms median. The end-to-end preparation job was 82.90 ms median (p95 114.25, max 262.61), leaving about 27.01 ms median unassigned to those measured stages, including request/pipe handoff and process scheduling. This confirms that moving work to another process does not solve the cadence problem: the API still withholds the whole four-sample batch until preparation, encoding, and transfer finish, and the added transfer protocol increases latency. Do not promote this path or change the original game clock to mask it.

The next investigation should measure an incremental, bounded sample-publication design in an isolated candidate: retain sequential ownership of the mutable per-pair road/history builder, publish each immutable sample as soon as ready, and let the consumer take only the next required sample. Preserve every source update, scene, sky owner, and ordering; do not drop frames or expose partial buffers. First verify race-free ordering and byte parity in a deterministic replay, then run matched full-scene-plus-sky timing. If incremental publication is not demonstrably better, return to thread-path stage and transition profiling rather than promote process mode.

### 2D backdrop/HUD path boundary (2026-10-11)

Inspected the current source composition path. `nf_gpu_draw` seeds the 3840×2160 target from the original 240×160 `nf_pixels()` framebuffer, draws the high-resolution polygon scene, then uploads and blends `nf_overlay` as a separate 240×160 texture. `scene_scanline` constructs that overlay as source-frame pixels that differ from the current BG2 backdrop. The 4K texture-pack lookup is called only while decoding native polygon textures; it never touches either the source framebuffer or the overlay. Thus the existing Graphics toggle cannot by itself remove pixelation from the sky/background, HUD, menus, or text in the standard `nf_gpu_draw` path. Other checkpoints document an experimental owned-sky/full-scene renderer with 4K continuous-angle interpolation; its unresolved gates are full-scene integration, cadence, and target-display validation, not absence of any candidate. The HUD/menu/text layer still lacks a complete 4K reconstruction and end-to-end parity proof. Next: resume measured cadence and visibility work on the existing owned-sky candidate, then separately derive and parity-check HUD/menu/text from captured layer snapshots while holding the GBA update timing fixed. Keep foreground text crisp and independently updated; do not temporally blend the whole screen without a layer mask.

### Native presentation source audit and next implementation boundary (2026-10-12)

Inspected `owned_native_source_display_span_worker_candidate.py`, `owned_native_source_timed_commit_adapter_candidate.py`, `owned_native_source_display_stats_session_candidate.py`, `owned_source_d3d_display_stats_candidate.py`, `owned_gpu_gl_display_cadence_candidate.c`, and `owned_draw_commit_candidate.c` against the latest 60-second pacing reports. The current “native source worker” owns the graphics context and native source builder, but its scheduler, job/future completion, packet copies, NumPy conversion, material upload, backdrop, sky, world/HUD draw calls, and separate present/abort commands remain orchestrated through Python. Thus the prior native notification FIFO did not remove the Python per-frame boundary, and the GIL-held commit experiment is not a viable workaround: it delayed original game updates and increased long presentation gaps.

This source audit narrows the next implementation target. Keep the emulation/update thread on its original clock and move the *whole prepared-scene-to-render-to-present transaction* under a native-owned bounded worker/ledger, rather than moving only counters or changing Python's switch interval. Each queued request must retain its immutable scene/context owner until completion, carry epoch/generation/display identity and deadline, allow pause/reset/close to cancel stale work safely, and record internal QPC stage times without calling back into Python. The main loop must never wait for GIL reacquisition or presentation bookkeeping. Preserve the full scene and changing sky; any capacity/latency behavior must be reported rather than hidden by dropping frames.

No product files were changed in this audit and no runtime timing test was run: source inspection was sufficient to expose the Python orchestration boundary, while prior foreground/physical-scanout checks remain unavailable in this automation desktop. Do not treat that or the source-worker prototype as acceptance.

### Sky freshness audit: framebuffer updates versus scene revisions (2026-10-12)

Ran a disposable candidate with `--test-realtime --original-timing --audit-layers` for 600 emulated updates. It completed in 10.053 seconds with 604 software draw/SwapBuffers iterations and zero GL errors. Per-display audit rows report 256 distinct full-source framebuffer hashes (255 adjacent transitions), 143 scene-version values/transitions in the 10-second run, and 141 adjacent changes in the diagnostic 21x19 source ROI. The ROI is not a validated semantic sky mask, so its cadence must not be called the skybox refresh rate. Several display iterations repeated the same emulated frame/source pixels; the run did not establish that the sky itself changes at 14, 25, or 60 Hz.

Source tracing explains the limits of the current host path. `nf_gpu_draw()` uploads the latest complete `nf_pixels()` framebuffer into the reference texture on each draw (`work/v2/gpu.c`, around line 372), while the reconstructed polygon interpolation updates its previous/current scene pair only when `nf_scene_version()` changes (around lines 323-365). There is no distinct sky-image interpolation in this active GPU path. Consequently, a ~60/s software presentation loop does not generate new sky content: it presents the most recently rendered GBA framebuffer and interpolates only eligible scene polygons between source revisions. This explains how a sky/background can look like it updates more slowly even while the host draws near 60/s, but the audit alone does not quantify the sky layer's exact cadence.

### DXGI frame-statistics timing: remaining batch-boundary stall traced (2026-10-12)

Rechecked the existing DXGI sync-interval-1 full-scene report `owned-native-1791798322714572300.json` and matched the long output interval to its scene-consumer and batch records. Across 3,583 original-timing updates and 3,595 full-scene/sky samples, DXGI frame statistics measured about 59.999 Hz across nearly 60 seconds, but `smooth_60fps_verified` remains false. Frame-statistics reported one steady-state 71.158 ms output gap at display index 1937 / source refresh 10675; the software callback timestamps measure a separate 59.203 ms interval for the same transition, so those two scopes must not be conflated.

The scene pair's scheduled deadline was 4474690640234 ns; its first draw began at 4474742458600 ns (51.818 ms late), and DXGI `Present(1)` began 54.573 ms late but returned in 1.430 ms. This rules out the DXGI call or draw time as the cause of that miss. The notification for refresh 10675 had been submitted at 4474588889400 ns and was not dequeued until 4474741309000 ns (152.420 ms later). The preceding batch's final committed sample completed at 4474687442500 ns, while the native batch call returned at 4474739655400 ns (52.113 ms afterward). Source inspection confirms the batch loop returns directly after its final successful sample; there is no explicit 52 ms wait after that sample. The evidence therefore narrows the stall to delayed consumer-thread progress at the end of a batch, with the queued notification waiting behind it. The report does not yet distinguish OS scheduling delay from Python/GIL reacquisition or another caller-side delay; do not state a definitive cause yet.

Next: add a test-only consumer trace for thread CPU time and QPC immediately around the native batch call and at its final commit/return boundary. If wall time grows while thread CPU does not, test consumer wake/GIL scheduling changes in an isolated candidate; if the native batch itself remains active, profile its internal stages. Preserve all source frames and original simulation timing; do not hide the missed output by dropping or retiming updates. Re-run the focused component/lifecycle checks after any candidate change, then repeat the measured cadence run before considering host integration.

The existing offscreen native-batch parity, pause/snapshot, full-motion, GPU-lifetime, and worker-reload tests passed earlier this continuation; they establish component behavior, not playable-host or 60-fps acceptance. Removed the unused duplicate D3D transaction adapter source from `prototype-runs/native-frame-transaction-20261012`; it was not integrated. The isolated DXGI sync-interval-1/frame-statistics bridge and wrapper remain for reproducibility. No production launcher/renderer, ROM, save, or stable fallback changed. ### Existing world-space wall identity path (2026-10-12)

- Source inspection found a better identity candidate than the screen-strip texture address. The legacy `scene_capture` path emits 2-pixel screen-column fragments (kind 3) with only texture pointer, shade, screen x/y, and UV. In contrast, the packaged `camera/live_scene.h` intercepts the original wall draw call, extracts each actual wall quad from the descriptor and consecutive source vertices, and appends it as a world-space scene surface. Its command identity is `{kind=2, world_state_pointer, source_vertex_record_pointer, source+44 animation/index, 0}`. `nf_extract_wall` validates the source record's index within the descriptor and obtains the next endpoint, so these fields are grounded in actual surface data rather than screen columns.

It is not yet proven stable across scene boundaries: state and source pointers may be reused, and `scene_assembly.c` stores supplied identities but does not itself perform cross-snapshot matching. A future world-space motion path must also bind surfaces to the coherent captured view/projection and reject mismatched scene epochs before rendering.

### Restored baseline RGB555-to-RGB888 palette conversion (2026-10-14)

The replay confirmed every changed output channel was +1 (8,356,372 channels; no negative deltas; maximum delta 1), matching this conversion difference.

**Source change.** Updated `work/camera/owned_decoded_texture.h` so `owned_palette_channel` uses `(value*255u)/31u`, with a comment documenting baseline compatibility. The known-good baseline DLL independently replays the same capture with 0 differences.

Two explicit modes preserve the established reference semantics:
- EXACT_ENDPOINTS: original even-byte source phases and exact original copies at alpha0/1; interior phase moves between those phases.
- CONTINUOUS_PHASE: original 14-bit angle sampled continuously at the same caller-supplied alpha, including subpixel phase at endpoints. This intentionally does NOT preserve original hardware-rounded endpoint pixels. It must not be described as byte-exact original sky rendering.

Both return two complete source-index spans plus a fractional weight. Future GPU code must apply historical palette lookup to EACH source texel and blend the resulting COLORS, never blend palette-index numbers. Original contiguous footprint starts at row44 and includes the16-byte final-row tail. Physical destination page switches at the exact new endpoint; display footprint stays unchanged. Buffer capacity, nonfinite alpha/mode and overlapping outputs reject before writes. Pair owns its asset after source capture/core close and is suitable for independent render-thread readers once publication ownership is established.

## 2026-10-17 — capture-reader ownership boundary audited for the optimization handoff

Read-only trace of `work\pc\source_reader.c` and `source_frame.c` clarified what the A/B profile measured. Each owner-thread packet request is serialized once into the reader's bounded scratch buffer; the second half of the two-call API copies that packet into a separately allocated `NFPCSourceFrame` blob. The frame must remain immutable and outlive the core while the render thread prepares it, so that copy currently provides the lifetime/thread-safety boundary. The reader's small key only validates the two phases of the current request; it does not reuse unchanged payloads between game frames. This explains why about 749 MB was copied during the 120-step capture-on sample without implying that the core serializes the same request twice.

No source changes were made. The previous A/B run remains the measured evidence: capture-on 55.4 steps/s, capture-off 59.4 steps/s on this AMD host, with correct mGBA tick checks in both and `full_scene_60fps` false. A sound optimization must keep packet snapshots consistent with their epoch/owner metadata and protect memory until render-thread preparation finishes. Likely review areas are a bounded leased slab/refcount pool, reducing repeated asset payloads while retaining dynamic histories, or a direct-final-buffer build API; each must preserve core-thread ownership, reset/toggle invalidation, and correct fallback on a missed capture. Do not simply point frames at the current scratch buffer, skip every other capture, or alter the game-step rate.

Status: PARTIALLY VERIFIED. This source audit sharpens the pending engineering task but changes no runtime behavior. Next step is Sol Medium-level design and implementation of an ownership-safe lower-copy snapshot path, followed by tests for concurrent prepare/reset/toggle, original-frame equivalence, and a full race timed at original mGBA cadence. Intel/NVIDIA laptop performance and audio/presentation symptoms still need the visible run report. Overall estimate remains about 68%; the synchronized 4K fallback remains available and separate from unfinished native full-scene 60-fps gameplay. Luna Low is still suitable for collecting the laptop report; Sol Medium remains recommended before the capture-path change.

## 2026-10-17 — captured the exact frame-ownership boundary for next design review

Read the live `source_frame.c` and `source_reader.c` after the fresh profile. `NFPCSourceFrame` individually owns its background and per-owner component allocations and is explicitly allowed to outlive/close over the core. `NFPCSourceReader` keeps a 64 MiB owner-thread scratch buffer, builds each packet once, then copies each packet into the separately owned frame; current profile counted 9,780,367,200 copied bytes over 1,200 native-mode steps. This copy is the lifetime/thread-safety boundary, not accidental duplicate copying. Reusing one mutable scratch pointer in published frames would be unsafe because the next game step would overwrite bytes while the render worker may still prepare them.

Next design review should compare (a) a bounded frame-owned arena/slab pool with explicit leases/retirement, and (b) a direct-to-final-frame serialization API after a cheap exact-size query. Any candidate must preserve the 64 MiB cap, packet keys/epoch validation, immutable worker access, reset/disable/toggle cleanup, and source-by-source exact parity. Measure capture and complete original-cadence elapsed time; retain the existing fallback until a candidate passes. No implementation was attempted under Luna Low because this is the architectural change already marked for Sol Medium review; the reviewed source layout and measured copy volume are now recorded to make that review concrete. Laptop-specific graphics/presentation diagnosis still depends on a session report from that Intel/NVIDIA machine. Project estimate remains about 68%.

## 2026-10-17 — verified the legacy texture identity algorithm against native material buffers

Inspected the older `v2/texture_pack.c`: each replacement filename is a 16-digit 64-bit FNV-1a hash over little-endian source width, source height, then every original RGBA8 source pixel; the payload header repeats that key and stores replacement dimensions. A correct native lookup must first reconstruct the original, unshaded source RGBA at its source dimensions using the exact source palette, calculate the same FNV-1a key, then use a validated replacement while preserving index-zero transparency, per-draw shading, and texture coordinates. The two formats cannot be connected by filename guessing or by hashing the upscaled output.

## 2026-10-17 — implemented and compiled bounded private-copy geometry cache component

Added maintained work/pc/geometry_packet_cache.c and .h plus test_geometry_packet_cache.c and .py. This is the storage/ownership component for the next optional core performance path. It is not wired into the producer, host or launchers yet. Entries use exact epoch/serial/begin/end/page fields plus caller-supplied exact guard bytes. Clear frees cache storage while previously returned frames remain valid.
